faqs.q: For functional prototypes, is FDM or SLA better?
faqs.a: If you need fit checks, durability tests, or functional trials, FDM is usually better. If looks and fine detail matter more, choose SLA or DLP.

faqs.q: SLA and DLP look similar—what is the difference?
faqs.a: Both are resin processes, but SLA cures point-by-point with a laser while DLP cures a full layer at once. For repeating small precision parts, DLP can be faster.

faqs.q: Which process is best when surface quality matters most?
faqs.a: For smooth surfaces and fine detail, pick SLA or DLP. FDM is more economical but layer lines can show.

faqs.q: How do SLS·SLM·DMLS differ from FDM?
faqs.a: Powder bed fusion can build complex shapes and metal parts without supports, but equipment and cost are higher. Everyday prototypes are often more economical with FDM·SLA·DLP.

faqs.q: What is the difference between PolyJet and SLA?
faqs.a: Both deliver high resolution. PolyJet/MJP jets materials and excels at multi-color/multi-material; SLA photopolymerizes resin and is widely used for fine detail and clear materials.

fdm.principle: Solid filament is heated and melted in a nozzle, then deposited layer by layer on the bed. The most widely used 3D printing technology.
strengths: Great for functional tests & assembly parts

sla.principle: A UV laser scans and selectively cures liquid photopolymer resin layer by layer. Surfaces are smooth with excellent detail.
strengths: Ideal for dental, jewelry & visual models

dlp.principle: A light source (projector/UV panel) cures an entire resin layer at once. Per-layer cure time is short, so builds can be faster than SLA.
strengths: Good for many identical small parts

powder-sintering.principle: Powder is spread thin and selectively sintered or melted by laser to build layers. Complex shapes can be made without supports; applies to plastics (SLS) and metals (SLM·DMLS).
strengths: Strong heat resistance for functional tests (by material)
Useful for low-volume multi-SKU metal parts
weaknesses: Equipment & operating cost higher than FDM/resin
Surface roughness & accuracy depend on post-processing
Metal workflows need more setup, safety & finishing

faqs.a: Yes. In WOW3D auto quote, choose “I don’t have a 3D model,” upload a JPG or PNG product photo, and AI builds a 3D mesh (STL) before volume and price quoting.

faqs.q: What photos work best for photo-to-3D modeling?
faqs.a: Prefer an object large and centered, a plain bright background, one object per shot, and low shadow or glare. Adding right, back, and left views can improve shape accuracy.

faqs.q: Can I order a print from an AI-generated 3D model?

faqs.q: Should I use photo → 3D or upload CAD/STL?

cards.title: Print process
cards.body: FDM, SLA, and DLP use different machine rates and materials, so the same model can quote differently.

cards.title: Layer & infill

cards.title: Print time

QuoteGuide.criteriaTitle: What drives a WOW3D auto quote
QuoteGuide.criteriaBody: 3D printing cost is not size alone. Upload a file and WOW3D calculates volume, surface area, dimensions, process, layer height, infill, and finishing in real time.
criteriaItems: Material: scales with filament or resin usage
Machine time: print duration × process hourly rate
Review adjustments: complex geometry, specialty materials, or deadline needs
QuoteGuide.layerBody: Lower layer heights need more layers, so print time goes up. For example FDM at 0.1 mm needs more layers and longer machine time than 0.2 mm—better surface detail, often a higher quote.
QuoteGuide.layerNote: 0.1 mm: detail first / 0.2 mm: standard / 0.3 mm: speed first

faqs.q: How is a 3D printing quote calculated?
faqs.a: WOW3D auto quotes combine material cost, machine time, layer height, infill, supports, and finishing. Time formulas and cost lines differ for FDM vs SLA/DLP.

faqs.q: Why does a lower layer height cost more?
faqs.a: Lower layers mean more layers for the same height, so print time increases. FDM at 0.1 mm needs more layers and longer machine time than 0.2 mm.

faqs.q: What is the difference between 20% and 100% infill?
faqs.a: Infill is internal density. Higher infill uses more material and time—raising the quote—but can suit parts that need strength and durability.

faqs.q: Should I choose FDM, SLA, or DLP?
faqs.a: Functional prototypes and durable parts usually fit FDM; surface quality and fine detail favor SLA or DLP. The best process depends on the goal, even for the same shape.

faqs.q: Can the auto quote differ from the final price?
faqs.a: Most typical models quote quickly, but complex geometry, specialty materials, finishing, or file issues may need admin review and a revised quote.

faqs.q: Can I get a quote without a 3D model file?
faqs.a: Yes. Upload a product photo (JPG/PNG), generate an AI 3D model, then continue to auto quote. For tight dimensional or assembly tolerances, prefer STL or STEP.

QuoteGuide.ctaBody: Upload STL, OBJ, or 3MF—or if you have no 3D file, use a product photo for AI 3D modeling, then check the quote.

faqs.q: Which file format is best for a quote?
faqs.a: STL, OBJ, 3MF, and PLY support instant auto quotes. STEP/STP convert on upload. STL is most common for geometry alone; OBJ or 3MF help when color or metadata matters.

faqs.q: Why won’t it print even though the file opens?
faqs.a: Often the mesh is not closed, faces are flipped, or walls are too thin for printing. Looking fine visually does not guarantee printability.

faqs.q: Can I upload STEP files?
faqs.a: Yes. STEP/STP convert on upload for quoting. If conversion is hard or geometry is complex, also prepare STL or 3MF.

faqs.q: What if I only have a photo?
faqs.a: Use photo → AI 3D in auto quote to build an STL from JPG/PNG, then quote and order. For tight tolerances, consider a modeling request.

cards.title: PLA
cards.body: Easy to print—great for general prototypes and education. Common for appearance checks, display, and early idea validation.

cards.title: ABS
cards.body: Better heat and impact resistance for housings, functional tests, and fit/assembly parts. Print environment control matters more.

cards.title: PETG
cards.body: Stronger than PLA and usually easier than ABS—often chosen as a balanced functional filament.

faqs.q: For beginners or general prototypes, which is best: PLA, ABS, or PETG?
faqs.a: PLA is usually the safest choice thanks to print stability and ease of use. For functional tests or more heat resistance, consider PETG or ABS.

faqs.q: If heat and impact matter, is ABS better than PLA?
faqs.a: Usually yes. ABS typically outdoes PLA on heat and impact—often a better fit for housings, functional test parts, and automotive or appliance prototypes.

faqs.q: Is PETG a middle ground between PLA and ABS?
faqs.a: In practice, often yes. PETG is stronger and more durable than PLA while usually easier to print than ABS, so it’s a popular balanced pick.

faqs.q: Which resin is best for design-review appearance prototypes?
faqs.a: Standard resin is used most for general appearance and design checks. Smooth surfaces and fine detail make it a strong fit for visual prototypes.

faqs.q: Is Tough better for assembly or functional tests?
faqs.a: Usually yes. Tough typically handles impact and load better than Standard—better for fit checks, fastening tests, and functional prototypes.

faqs.q: Should I pick Clear resin for transparent parts or window structures?
faqs.a: Yes. Covers, windows, and observation parts that need visibility suit Clear. For high clarity you may still need polishing or coating.

faqs.q: Which material is used most for prototypes—PLA, ABS, or PETG?
faqs.a: It depends on the goal. Appearance prototypes often use PLA; parts that need durability usually use PETG or ABS.

faqs.q: Do I need a strong material if I only need a design check?
faqs.a: No. For size and form only, economical options with good surface quality—like PLA or Standard resin—are often more efficient.

faqs.q: For assembly tests, is FDM better than resin?
faqs.a: Often yes for repeated fastening, housing tests, and functional review—ABS or PETG FDM parts are a common fit. For precise fit checks, Tough resin can also work well.

faqs.q: Can 3D printing really make transparent parts?
faqs.a: Yes, but results vary a lot by process and finishing. Clear resin is usually best; glass-like clarity often needs extra polishing and coating.

faqs.q: For clear covers or windows, is PETG or Clear resin better?
faqs.a: If visibility and appearance matter most, choose Clear resin. If strength and general function matter more and slight translucency is OK, PETG is a solid option.

faqs.q: Is post-processing required for transparent parts?
faqs.a: Usually yes if you want high clarity. Resin parts improve with wash, cure, polish, and coating.

items.detail: Strong for impact and heat when fastening or assembly tests matter. Good machinability and finishing make it common for housing prototypes.

items.detail: A good balance of strength, durability, and print stability for protective cases, covers, and general exterior parts—often easier to print than ABS.

faqs.q: For electronics housings or cases, is ABS or PETG better?
faqs.a: If heat resistance, assembly, and finishing matter most, ABS is often better. For print stability plus balanced durability, PETG is a strong choice.

faqs.q: Are small precision cases better in resin?
faqs.a: If dimensional accuracy and surface quality come first, Tough resin can help. For repeated fastening or impact resistance, prefer ABS or PETG.

faqs.q: Should appearance mockups and functional cases use different materials?
faqs.a: Yes. Appearance mockups can use PLA or Standard resin, but protective cases and housings for real use usually need stronger options like PETG, ABS, or Tough resin.

items.detail: Often the first review for functional parts that need both heat and impact resistance—common for housings, fastening parts, and test structures.

faqs.q: What material is best when both heat and impact resistance are required?
faqs.a: ABS is usually reviewed first. Strong assembly, finishing, and functional-test suitability make it common for heat- and impact-demanding parts.

faqs.q: Is PETG weaker than ABS?
faqs.a: It depends on the metric. PETG is excellent for print stability and general durability and is often easier to handle than ABS. For higher heat resistance or certain functional tests, ABS may still win.

faqs.q: Can precise functional parts be made in Tough resin?
faqs.a: Yes for small precision parts or prototype review. Under continuous load, heat, and repeated impact, FDM materials like ABS or PETG are often a better fit.

MaterialsSafety.metaDescription: WOW3D material safety guidance for FDM (PLA, ABS, PETG, TPU) and resin (SLA/DLP): handling, ventilation, storage, and disposal.
MaterialsSafety.ogDescription: Handling, ventilation, storage, and disposal guidance for FDM and resin materials.
MaterialsSafety.title: Material Safety Information
MaterialsSafety.subtitle: Safety practices for handling, storing, and disposing of FDM filaments and UV resins used in WOW3D PRO.
MaterialsSafety.noticeBody: Composition and hazard levels vary by manufacturer and formulation. Ask the material maker or supplier for the exact Safety Data Sheet (SDS/MSDS). This page summarizes general 3D printing material practices.
MaterialsSafety.msdsBefore: SDS/MSDS documents and manufacturer-specific safety instructions come from each material’s maker or supplier. WOW3D PRO may use materials from multiple brands — to confirm exact product name, batch, and manufacturer, ask when ordering or via

items.label: Purpose
items.text: Minimum practices to reduce risks when handling, storing, and disposing of FDM filaments (PLA, ABS, PETG, TPU) and UV-curable resins for SLA/DLP, and to maintain a safer workspace.

items.label: Scope
items.text: Based on materials WOW3D Co., Ltd. uses for WOW3D PRO production. Composition can vary by maker and batch — check the manufacturer SDS when purchasing or using materials.

items.label: Hot nozzle & heated bed
items.text: Melt temperatures (typically 180–260°C) can cause burns. Do not touch parts during or immediately after printing.

items.label: Ventilation
items.text: Melting/layering may release ultrafine particles (UFPs) or VOCs. Keep good ventilation (natural or local exhaust); for long sessions, consider an exhaust hood or air cleaner.

items.label: Storage
items.text: Avoid moisture, direct sun, and heat. Sealed, humidity-controlled containers help preserve filament life and quality.

items.label: Food & oral contact
items.text: Do not use FDM prints for food or oral contact unless the material and coating are approved for that use. Some PLA/PETG products are food-contact grade, but surface roughness, cracks, and bacteria risk make ordinary prints unsuitable for food use.

materials.name: PLA (polylactic acid)
materials.summary: Plant-derived and often biodegradable; typically lower emissions and milder odor.
materials.notes: Melt ~180–220°C; ventilation recommended; heat/moisture storage can degrade performance; dispose per general plastic or designated biodegradable rules.

materials.name: ABS (acrylonitrile-butadiene-styrene)
materials.summary: Styrene/VOCs may be released at high melt temperatures — adequate ventilation is essential.
materials.notes: Melt ~220–260°C; ventilate/exhaust to avoid odor and fumes; avoid long use in sealed unventilated spaces; some regions apply workplace exposure limits for ABS fumes.

materials.name: PETG
materials.summary: Between PLA and ABS; some fine emissions possible at high temperature.
materials.notes: Melt ~220–250°C; maintain normal ventilation; watch moisture uptake and dry storage; food/medical grades exist but limits depend on production and finishing.

materials.name: TPU (thermoplastic polyurethane)
materials.summary: Flexible material; high-temperature emissions are often relatively lower than some others, but ventilation is still recommended for hot prints.
materials.notes: Melt ~210–240°C; keep ventilation; long moisture/UV exposure can age the material.

items.label: Uncured resin
items.text: Liquid resin contains photoinitiators and monomers that can irritate skin/eyes or cause allergies. Wear nitrile gloves and safety glasses (or a face shield). Wash skin with soap and water immediately; if in eyes, rinse thoroughly and seek medical care.

items.label: Inhalation
items.text: Avoid inhaling resin odor/fumes; keep the workspace ventilated (e.g., exhaust hood).

items.label: Curing (UV / sunlight)
items.text: Resin cures under UV. Keep uncured resin away from direct sun and UV lamps; use opaque containers for storage and transport.

items.label: Storage
items.text: Avoid direct sun and heat; keep lids tightly closed. Check manufacturer shelf life / use-by dates.

items.label: Fully cured parts
items.text: Fully washed and cured parts are lower risk than uncured resin, but for food, oral, or prolonged skin contact confirm food-contact / biocompatibility with the manufacturer.

sections.title: 5. Notes by resin type
sections.intro: Hardness, strength, viscosity, and cure conditions differ for Standard, Tough, Clear, Flexible, and similar resins. Apply the common resin practices above and follow each maker’s SDS and instructions.

items.label: Standard
items.text: Handle with ordinary eye protection, gloves, and ventilation.

items.label: Tough
items.text: Formulation may differ due to strength additives — check the manufacturer SDS.

items.label: Clear
items.text: Higher UV transmission — be extra careful about light exposure during cure and storage.

items.label: Flexible
items.text: May include plasticizers; follow manufacturer guidance.

items.label: Ventilation
items.text: Indoors, use open windows, fans, local exhaust, or air cleaners to bring in fresh air and reduce fumes/dust.

items.label: Storage
items.text: Keep away from children and pets; avoid sun, heat, and open flames. Store resin in opaque containers.

items.label: Disposal
items.text: Follow local recycling / designated waste rules for used filament, resin, and cured byproducts. Dispose of resin bottles and uncured residue per maker and local guidance.

items.label: Emergencies
items.text: For severe burns, eye/skin irritation, or symptoms after inhalation, seek medical care immediately and share SDS/ingredient info when possible.
